Which Georgia office does what on a property tax bill?

The assessor values, and the commissioner collects. Each of Georgia's 159 counties has a board of tax assessors that sets appraised value and hears disputes, plus a tax commissioner who bills for the county and school system and, in some counties, for cities too.

Revenue's Local Government Services Division sits above both. It approves county digests, certifies local officials and audits every board, yet it says it cannot override a board, hearing officer, arbitrator or court on a single home. Questions about worth belong with the assessor. Questions about the amount owed belong with the commissioner.

How does Georgia arrive at the taxable figure for a home?

The state taxes two-fifths of a home's fair market value, which is the 40 percent assessment level. Fair market value means an arm's length bona fide price between a knowledgeable buyer and a willing seller.

Revenue's formula subtracts exemptions from the assessed figure and then applies the local millage rate. Georgia law has every property valued again each year as of January 1 (O.C.G.A. 48-5-6, 48-5-2), and no statewide revaluation calendar exists. Counties compare their digests with recent sales and adjust values that look off, so a booming county can reprice quickly while a quiet one barely moves.

Millage is local, set separately for the county, the city and the school district. Look at the rates printed on your own bill.

What is the Georgia property tax due date?

Bills are generally payable by December 20 unless a statute sets another date.

  • A few counties pick an earlier deadline or split payment into two installments.
  • The state FAQ says billing starts a 60-day payment period.
  • Land that straddles two counties is taxed through the one holding most of it, and that office forwards the other county's share.

Pay-online options exist in some counties only, so call the commissioner's office to see what yours takes.

Must owners file a return every year in Georgia?

No. Returns are taken until April 1 (O.C.G.A. 48-5-18), yet an owner who filed or paid the previous year is treated as returning the same property at the same value with the same exemptions.

The same treatment reaches a buyer who paid real estate transfer tax last year. New improvements change the picture, because a fresh return should follow in the year they appear, and homestead still needs its own form. Returns go to county officials, never to the state.

How does an owner contest a Georgia assessment?

The written appeal goes to the county assessors, and a 45-day clock starts from the mailing date printed on the notice. Accepted grounds are taxability, value, uniformity and a denied exemption. The state's uniform form is PT-311A, and mailing it to the state agency leaves the appeal unprotected.

Appeal routes described on the Revenue Department's appeal page
RouteWho can use itWhat follows
Board of EqualizationAny ownerAssessors may revise and reissue the notice, which can be appealed within 30 days; if not revised, a hearing is set
Hearing officerNon-homestead real property over $500,000, value or uniformity onlyDecision can go to superior court
ArbitratorValue disputes, backed by a certified appraisal due within 45 days after the board acknowledges the appealHearing within 30 days; the side whose value lies farther from the arbitrator's pays costs

To reach superior court, the owner mails or files written notice with the assessors, and the deadline is 30 days from the decision. The court will not hear the case until taxes equal to the last determined year are paid (O.C.G.A. 48-5-29). An owner who ends with a value at or below 85 percent of the figure set below also recovers litigation costs and attorney fees.

How does Georgia's arbitration option work in practice?

The schedule is short and appraisal-driven. An owner who picks arbitration on the form gets an acknowledgment from the assessors within 10 days, then has 45 days to supply a certified appraisal of the property.

The assessors may accept the appraisal or reject it. A rejection sends the appeal to the appeal administrator, the chief or presiding superior court judge authorizes the arbitration, and a hearing follows within 30 days. The arbitrator rules at the end of the hearing, and either side may carry the result to superior court. Cost-shifting adds risk: if the arbitrator lands closer to the owner's value the county pays, and if closer to the assessors' value the owner pays.

What happens if the case reaches a Georgia superior court?

The assessors certify the appeal papers to the court clerk after the owner's filing fees are paid, and the state says most appeals are heard by a jury at the first term of court unless a question of law is involved.

Ahead of that, the assessors have 45 days to schedule a settlement conference, which must happen no later than 30 days after their notice, with both sides conferring in good faith. If no agreement on value emerges, the assessors tell the owner in writing to pay court filing fees to the clerk within 20 days.

What did HB 581 and the 2026 legislation change?

HB 581 created a statewide floating homestead exemption, and 2026 laws reshape how it and the notice of assessment work. The Revenue Department's May 2026 legislative update lists the main items.

  • SB 33, the HOME Act of 2026, ends the HB 581 opt-out and makes a statewide floating exemption apply starting January 1, 2027, using 2026 values as the baseline.
  • SB 566 standardizes the assessment notice: an explicit fair market value statement, estimated savings from exemptions, a named appeal contact and a reminder that homestead can be claimed during the appeal window.
  • Report a lost homestead eligibility before the appeal period ends, because the update says tax plus a 50 percent penalty stays with the property.
  • HB 974 funds Homeowner Tax Relief Grants of $18,000 per eligible homestead, applied for through the digest process.

The update also contrasts two local sales tax tools. PTRLOST and FLOST, collected in 35 counties, lower property tax across all property types. LHOST requires a local act and a referendum and mainly benefits homesteads.

Who owes tax when a Georgia house changes hands?

Whoever held title on January 1 owes that year's bill, and the state says no refund follows for the months after an owner sells and moves. Contracts therefore split the year at closing.

Call the commissioner for a payoff number before the sale date. Liens are recorded by the county clerk on the general execution docket. Ask the commissioner about a county lien, and the Compliance Division or a regional Revenue office about a state lien.

Transfer tax is a separate levy that must be paid before the superior court clerk records a deed. The statute assigns it to the seller, though a purchase contract may move it to the buyer.

Frequently asked questions

What share of a home's market value does Georgia tax?

Forty percent. Revenue puts the assessed value at that share of market value, and exemptions are subtracted from the assessed amount.

What if I missed the appeal deadline on my notice?

The window is 45 days counted from the mailing date on the notice. Call the assessors to learn whether anything is still open for that notice, and watch for the next year's mailing.

Where do I send the PT-311A appeal form?

To the county board of tax assessors. Email is accepted only where that board has adopted a written policy consenting to electronic service, and the state revenue agency should never receive it.

Will the state refund tax for the months after I sell?

No. Under the state's FAQ, whoever owned the property on January 1 answers for the whole year, and partial-year residents get nothing back.

Should I call the commissioner or the assessor about a tax problem?

Call the commissioner for bills, payments and, in many counties, homestead filing. Call the assessor for value, appeals and digest records.

Who is eligible for a Georgia homestead exemption?

An owner who holds the home and lives in it as a legal residence on the first day of the tax year. The state tax agency cites O.C.G.A. 48-5-40 for that test and adds that the owner must actually occupy the house.

A training deck from the agency's digest compliance unit fills in the edges. Title can be a fee interest, a life estate or a contract of purchase, even with a mortgage on it. The deed has to be on record before the application goes in. A person owning two houses gets the exemption on one only, and a family group gets one homestead.

  • Joint owners who all live there can each claim, and an occupant who shares title may claim the full amount.
  • Absence for health reasons does not forfeit the exemption, and a relative or friend can alert the tax office.
  • A house damaged by fire, flood or storm stays classed as a homestead for a year while the owner lives elsewhere.
  • Children living in the home of a deceased or incapacitated parent can qualify, whether or not the estate has been distributed.

Where do you file, and how late can you apply?

File with the county tax commissioner, or with the assessor's office where the county has delegated that task. The state form is labeled LGS-Homestead, and it may be submitted at any point in the year.

April 1 used to be the hard cutoff, matching the return deadline. The agency now says owners may apply after that date, up to the end of their 45-day window to contest the assessment notice. A missed filing is treated as a waiver for the year.

Re-filing is not an annual chore. The agency's returns page explains that an owner who filed or paid the prior year is treated as claiming the same exemptions again. The 2026 legislative update adds that new assessment notices must mention the appeal-window option and ask owners to report any loss of eligibility.

What does the standard exemption take off a Georgia bill?

Two thousand dollars of assessed value. The deduction comes from the 40 percent assessed amount (O.C.G.A. 48-5-44) and reaches county and school levies, but not school taxes charged by cities or levies that retire bonded debt.

That figure is modest, so a local exemption often matters more. The Constitution lets counties pass their own, and the agency says county exemptions tend to be more generous than the state's. Ask the tax commissioner which ones attach to your parcel.

Which exemptions exist for older owners and veterans?

The state offers several, each tied to its own code section and tests.

State homestead exemptions listed on the Revenue Department homestead page
ExemptionTerms as printedCode section

Age 62 or older, floatingInflation-proof county exemption when household income is no more than $30,00048-5-47.1

In the income tests, retirement, pension and disability income is left out up to the Social Security maximum, listed as $96,432 for 2025.

Disabled veteran details from the agency's deck:

  • The veteran files once in the county of residence, and the exemption then renews itself.
  • It extends to an unremarried surviving spouse or minor children who stay in the home.
  • A retroactive VA eligibility finding can bring a refund for up to three prior tax years.

How does the floating base-year exemption work?

It shelters growth in assessed value above a fixed base, within an inflation allowance. The statute is O.C.G.A. 48-5-44.2, created by HB 581, and for homes first receiving it in 2025 the base is the 2024 assessed value.

The base may rise each year by up to the inflation rate the Revenue Commissioner sets, often measured with a federal price index. Coverage reaches only the primary residence and at most five contiguous acres. It renews by itself while the owner lives there, is added on top of other homestead exemptions, and gives way to a larger local floating exemption where one exists. A surviving spouse who stays keeps it, and no later owner inherits it.

Owners with a 2024 homestead who stayed eligible received it automatically for 2025, and everyone else applied once. The May 2026 update then describes SB 33, the HOME Act of 2026, as removing the opt-out for local governments, with a statewide floating exemption from January 1, 2027 on 2026 baseline values.

Can heirs or a surviving spouse keep a homestead exemption on an inherited Georgia house?

Often yes, when someone actually lives there. The department's deck describes a code section covering homes with several titleholders and homes held by administrators, executors or trustees, which allows the exemption where legal title sits with several owners and one or more heirs living in the house claim it in the manner provided by law.

A surviving spouse has added protection. The deck says that if the assessors intend to deny the exemption, they must send notice, and the spouse then has 30 days from the notice to apply for the amount the spouse is entitled to. A person denied an exemption can appeal under O.C.G.A. 48-5-311.

Which Georgia counties use a valuation freeze?

The state's page names Baldwin, Barrow, Camden, Carroll, Chatham, Cherokee, Clarke, Cobb, Dade, DeKalb, Douglas, Effingham, Fannin, Floyd, Forsyth, Fulton, Gilmer, Glynn, Greene, Gwinnett, Habersham, Henry, Liberty, McIntosh, Meriwether, Murray, Muscogee, Oconee, Pierce, Putnam, Toombs, Towns, Walton, Ware and White counties, plus the City of Atlanta.

A freeze holds the taxable base at a starting value while the owner remains in the home, and certain counties allow it to grow by a set percentage. Terms differ, so the local tax office has the final word.

What becomes of the exemption when the house sells?

For the year of sale, it can stay with the seller. An Attorney General opinion quoted in the agency's deck says an owner who occupied the home on January 1 and otherwise qualified may claim the exemption even after moving out later that year.

The benefit does not move to the buyer. A new owner who plans to live in the home needs to own and occupy it on a later January 1 and file on time. Sellers who rented the house out should speak with the tax commissioner before closing, since the 2026 update says unreported ineligibility carries tax plus a 50 percent penalty that attaches to the property rather than the person.

Frequently asked questions

Is April 1 still the deadline for a Georgia homestead exemption?

April 1 remains the traditional date, but the state says owners can apply up to the end of the 45-day appeal window. Your county tax office can say which date it applies.

Do I reapply for the exemption every year?

No. An owner who filed or paid the year before is treated as claiming it again. Failure to file the first time is a waiver, and you must tell the tax commissioner if you stop qualifying.

Can a rental house get the exemption?

No. The home must be your actual residence and domicile. The deck cites an Attorney General opinion denying it to an owner who rented out a house and kept part for storage.

Does a buyer take over my exemption?

No. The floating exemption does not pass to a later owner, and a buyer must own and live in the home on a January 1 to qualify for the year.

Which office takes the application where I live?

The county tax commissioner in most counties, or the board of tax assessors in some. The state's County Property Tax Facts page tells you which official to call.

How does foreclosure work in Georgia?

Georgia is a non-judicial foreclosure state, so a lender holding a deed to secure debt can sell the home at auction without suing the borrower or appearing before a judge. The Attorney General's mortgage page points to O.C.G.A. 44-14-162 through 44-14-162.4 for the procedure.

Two papers sit behind the process. The promissory note is the borrower's promise to repay, and the deed to secure debt, which most people call the mortgage, gives the lender the legal right to take the house if the note goes unpaid. A default is usually missed payments, though the Attorney General notes it can also be a lapse in property insurance or unpaid property taxes.

What notice does a Georgia borrower get before the sale?

The borrower must be sent written notice at least 30 days before the proposed sale date, by registered or certified mail or statutory overnight delivery with return receipt, and the notice must carry a copy of the sale advertisement. It also has to name a person or entity with authority to negotiate, amend and modify the loan, with an address and telephone number.

Refusing a certified letter does not cancel the notice. The lender must also run the sale advertisement in the county's official legal newspaper once a week for four consecutive weeks, and if it has not already done so it must file proof of its ownership of the security instrument, usually an assignment, with the superior court clerk before the sale starts. That filing is one way a borrower can find out who holds the loan now.

When and where are Georgia foreclosure sales held?

Sales happen on the courthouse steps of the county where the property sits, on the first Tuesday of the month between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. The Attorney General's consumer page adds that when the first Tuesday is a holiday the sale moves to the first Wednesday.

Bidding is open to the public, but the lender is frequently the only bidder. The lender signs a deed of foreclosure to the winning bidder, which may be the lender itself, and at that point the winner becomes the owner.

What is the sequence from default to the courthouse steps?

Georgia power of sale foreclosure sequence from the Georgia Attorney General mortgage and foreclosure pages
StepWhat the lender must doTiming

Notice to borrowerWritten notice by certified mail, registered mail or overnight deliveryAt least 30 days before the sale

What can a homeowner do before the sale date?

Atlanta Legal Aid lists six ways a scheduled sale can be stopped, and each one should be confirmed in writing from the lender. A borrower who reaches an agreement should insist on a written confirmation that the sale is cancelled.

  • Reinstate the loan by paying the missed payments, attorney fees and foreclosure costs
  • Agree to a payment plan or loan modification
  • Sell the home and pay the mortgage off in full before the scheduled sale
  • Complete a short sale or deed in lieu of foreclosure, which the lender must approve
  • File bankruptcy before the sale, which stays a non-judicial foreclosure
  • Win a temporary restraining order by showing a legal basis, such as a notice defect

The Attorney General cautions that applying for a modification may not stop a sale, since homes have been sold while an application was still pending. Active duty service members may have extra protection under the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act.

Can I sell my Georgia house before the foreclosure sale?

Yes, a sale that pays the loan in full before the scheduled date is one of the options on the legal aid flyer, and it keeps the foreclosure off the table. Sellers who owe more than the house will bring should know that a short sale needs lender approval and can carry tax or deficiency consequences, so ask a lawyer or HUD certified housing counselor before agreeing.

A seller pays the state real estate transfer tax unless the contract says otherwise. The Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority prints the rate as $1 for the first $1,000 and 10 cents for each additional $100 or fractional part of $100, due before the deed can be recorded. The Census Bureau counts 65.7 percent of Georgia homes as owner occupied for 2020 to 2024, and median monthly owner costs with a mortgage at $1,783.

Who can help a Georgia homeowner facing foreclosure?

Start by gathering the closing papers, lender letters, mortgage statements and payment records, because a housing counselor or lawyer will ask for them first. A borrower who spots an error can send a written request to the servicer under the federal Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, and the Attorney General says the servicer must acknowledge it within twenty days and answer within sixty.

Free legal help is available through Atlanta Legal Aid, which keeps offices for Fulton, DeKalb, Cobb, South Fulton and Clayton, and Gwinnett residents, and through the Georgia Legal Services Program for other counties. A HUD certified housing counselor may also be able to review the options with the homeowner.

What happens to the borrower after the foreclosure sale?

A valid foreclosure ends the borrower's right to live in the house, and the new owner can file a dispossessory action if the former owner stays. Legal aid describes the sequence: a demand to leave, a warrant that may be posted on the door, seven days to answer, a hearing about a week later, and seven days to move once a judge rules against the occupant.

Some buyers offer cash for keys in exchange for leaving the home empty and broom clean by a set date. In most cases the lender accepts the property as payment and the matter ends. The lender may instead sue for the gap between the sale price and the loan balance, which is called a deficiency proceeding and goes before the courts. Anyone who suspects a wrongful foreclosure should seek an attorney or legal aid quickly, and Atlanta Legal Aid's Home Defense Program can be reached at (770) 817-7538.

Watch for rescue scams. Legal aid warns about offers that take upfront fees, trick owners into signing over title, or promise that recording a document in the deed records will halt a sale. The Attorney General's page also warns against signing over a deed to save a home and against sending mortgage payments to anyone other than the holder.

Frequently asked questions

How much notice does a Georgia lender have to give before foreclosing?

At least 30 days in writing before the proposed sale date. The notice goes by registered or certified mail or statutory overnight delivery, and it must include a copy of the sale advertisement and contact details for someone with authority to modify the loan.

What day are foreclosure sales held in Georgia?

The first Tuesday of each month, between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m., on the courthouse steps of the county where the home sits. The Attorney General's consumer page says a holiday moves the sale to the first Wednesday.

Does Georgia require a court case to foreclose?

No. Georgia is a non-judicial foreclosure state, and a lender can use the power of sale in the deed to secure debt without filing suit. A borrower who believes the process was flawed can go to court, for example to seek a restraining order.

Can a lender still sue me after the house is sold at foreclosure?

Yes, for any shortfall. The Attorney General's page says the holder may sue for the difference between the foreclosure price and what was owed on the note, called a deficiency proceeding. In most cases the lender simply keeps the property as satisfaction of the loan.

Will filing bankruptcy stop a Georgia foreclosure sale?

A properly filed bankruptcy petition stays a non-judicial foreclosure if it reaches the bankruptcy clerk before the property is sold. The lender may ask the bankruptcy judge for permission to resume, and the owner must keep paying the mortgage to keep the house. Talk to an attorney first because the filing has lasting effects.

Is there any Georgia estate or inheritance tax left?

No. Georgia collects neither, and the Department of Revenue's estate tax FAQ opens with the statute that ended it.

O.C.G.A. 48-12-1 took effect July 1, 2014. Its first subsection says that from that date no estate taxes are levied by the state and no state estate tax returns are required. The FAQ also states flatly that Georgia has no inheritance tax, a term some people use for the estate tax.

A family selling an inherited Georgia house therefore faces no state charge on the estate itself before the property is sold or passed to heirs. What remains is tied to the sale, to the property, and to federal law.

What happened to the old Georgia estate tax?

It lives on only for estates of people who died before January 1, 2005. The Department explains that the tax was built on the federal credit for state death taxes shown on Form 706.

Congress phased that credit down for deaths in 2002, 2003 and 2004, then replaced it with a deduction for deaths in 2005 and after. Because Georgia's tax rode on the credit, an estate with a date of death after December 31, 2004 owes nothing to the state in any year when federal law allows no state death tax credit.

For the older estates, the FAQ gives these mechanics:

  • The estate pays the tax before assets reach heirs, and the heirs do not pay it.
  • Georgia has no form of its own: the filer sends a copy of the federal return with payment, due 9 months after the date of death.
  • Interest for months starting on or after July 1, 2016 runs at the Federal Reserve prime rate plus 3 percent a year.
  • The Department can grant extra time to pay on the same terms as IRC section 6161, but it does not offer the installment option for family farms and closely held businesses under section 6166.
  • The Department issues a certificate of payment, and it does not issue a closing letter of its own.

Files for those estates go to the Estate Tax Section at 2595 Century Parkway NE, Atlanta 30345-3173.

How did the old tax treat property in more than one state?

The Department's FAQ answers this with a proportion. For the estate of a nonresident who owned Georgia property, the gross value of the Georgia property is divided by the total federal gross estate, and that percentage is multiplied by the total allowable state death tax credit to reach the Georgia tax. A worksheet or cover letter shows the computation.

For a Georgia resident whose estate also owed tax to other states, the same idea runs in reverse: the value taxable elsewhere over the federal gross estate gives the share by which the Georgia tax is reduced. No deductions are used when prorating the credit, although the estate still gets indirect benefit from the marital deduction and mortgage deductions through the federal credit.

  • Extension to file: attach payment to a copy of the federal extension request, marked as the Georgia copy, when tax is estimated to be due.
  • Amended federal return: send Georgia a copy, and a refund claim is held until the IRS settles the change.
  • Refund of an estimate: attach a letter to the Georgia copy of the return when filing.

These rules only matter for deaths before 2005. If the date of death is unclear, check it against the 2005 cutoff before assuming anything, and write to the Estate Tax Section.

Could the federal estate tax apply to a Georgia house?

Only for estates large enough to cross the IRS threshold. For deaths in 2026 the IRS table lists $15,000,000, and smaller estates generally skip the return unless a spouse's portability election is wanted.

A Georgia house enters the calculation at its fair market value on the date of death, alongside everything else the person owned. Debts, administration costs and property left to a surviving spouse or a qualified charity can be deducted.

Federal estate tax filing threshold by year of death, as printed on the IRS estate tax page
Year of deathReturn required if amount exceeds
2023$12,920,000

What tax questions come up when an heir sells the house?

Three of them recur: income, gain, and the annual property bill. Georgia's lack of an estate tax removes a fourth.

  • Income: the Department tells heirs to ask the IRS whether anything inherited counts as income.
  • Gain: profit is the sale price minus adjusted basis, and the IRS sends owners of inherited property to its basis publications.
  • Home exclusion: the $250,000 or $500,000 exclusion requires 24 months of ownership and use inside the five-year window, which an heir who never lived there may lack.
  • Property tax: the January 1 owner is on the hook for the year.

A brokerage that asks for a Georgia tax waiver before moving inherited stock can be told the Department says Georgia has no inheritance or estate tax waiver requirements.

Who owes the property tax bill on an inherited house?

The owner of record on January 1 carries the year, and the state offers no refund for a partial year. If the owner died partway through the year, the estate or the selling heir still has to resolve that bill.

Counties pick their own due dates. The usual date is December 20, with 60 days after billing to pay, but Fulton County, for one, set October 15, 2026 for most of its 2026 bills.

Before you list, call the county tax commissioner for the balance on the parcel. Ask too whether anything has been filed against the property on the clerk's general execution docket, since county tax liens are recorded there.

Do out-of-state heirs face withholding on a Georgia sale?

Often they do. Under O.C.G.A. 48-7-128 a nonresident seller has 3% of the price withheld, or 3% of the gain after signing the Form IT-AFF2 affidavit.

The exemptions include prices under $20,000 and cases where the tax would be below $600 with a signed gain affidavit. Co-owners are tested one at a time, so a resident heir and a nonresident heir are treated separately and only the nonresident share is affected. The buyer files by the end of the month after closing and gives the seller a statement for the Georgia return.

Have your settlement agent confirm each heir's residency before the closing statement is drawn up.

Frequently asked questions

Does Georgia tax inheritances?

No. The Department of Revenue states that Georgia has no inheritance tax, and O.C.G.A. 48-12-1 bars state estate taxes and state estate tax returns from July 1, 2014.

When did Georgia stop collecting an estate tax?

The statute took effect July 1, 2014. The Department adds that the old tax reached only deaths before January 1, 2005, because the federal credit it relied on turned into a deduction afterward.

Is a tax waiver needed to move inherited stock out of a Georgia decedent's name?

No. The Department says Georgia has no inheritance or estate tax waiver requirements. A brokerage that asks for one can be pointed to the Department's FAQ.

Do I file a federal estate tax return for a Georgia estate?

Only for large estates. The IRS lists $15,000,000 for deaths in 2026, counted on the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption. A return can also be filed to elect portability for a surviving spouse.

Who pays property tax if the owner died during the year?

The bill follows ownership on January 1, and Georgia allows no refund to partial-year owners. The estate or the selling heir should get the balance from the county tax commissioner and settle it with the closing.

Georgia evictions are called dispossessory actions and run through county courts.

What is the Georgia eviction process called, and where does it run?

Georgia calls it a dispossessory proceeding, and the landlord starts it by filing a sworn affidavit, sometimes called the eviction warrant, asking the court to return the property and award unpaid rent. Georgia Courts explains that without that filing and a court order a landlord has no legal way to remove a tenant.

Most of these cases are filed in magistrate court because that court can be easier to navigate and may move faster. The handbook notes they can also go to state or superior court, or to some municipal courts, and a few magistrate courts take filings online. The case belongs in the county where the rental house sits.

What does the landlord's affidavit have to say?

It must be made under oath and carry five items, according to the handbook. A landlord who leaves one out gives the tenant an easy argument that the case is defective.

  • The landlord's name and the tenant's name
  • The reason the tenant is being removed
  • A statement that possession was demanded and refused, plus the three day rent notice where rent is the issue
  • The amount of rent or other money claimed, if any

Attaching the lease or proof of past payments is a common way to show how the amount was reached.

How are the court papers delivered to the tenant?

The summons can be served three ways: by handing it to the tenant, by leaving it with a competent adult who lives in the unit, or by tack and mail. The handbook calls tack and mail the most common method, and it is allowed only when nobody was home when the sheriff tried personal delivery. The postmark date on the envelope should match the day the copy went on the door, and if it does not, the tenant may be able to argue the service was insufficient.

Service method matters for money. When service was by tack and mail and the tenant never answers or appears, the court may still order the tenant to leave but cannot award rent or other damages to the landlord. In most counties the sheriff handles service, though the legal aid flyer notes that in some places a county marshal delivers the warrant.

What are the steps and timing from filing to move-out?

Stages of a Georgia dispossessory case from the DCA Landlord-Tenant Handbook and the Georgia Legal Aid foreclosure flyer
StageWhat happensTiming stated in the source
FilingLandlord swears out the affidavit in the county of the rentalAfter demand is refused
ServiceSheriff or marshal delivers or tacks and mails the summonsDate of service starts the clock
AnswerTenant states defenses and counterclaims, orally or in writingSeven days from service
Rent into courtCourt may order rent paid in if no decision is reachedAfter two weeks without a ruling
HearingHeld when a valid defense is raisedUsually within seven days
Writ of possessionLandlord requests it after a win; sheriff supervises removalTenant moves after seven days

What should a tenant put in the answer?

Every defense and every counterclaim, because Georgia treats anything left out as hard to raise later. A tenant can write the answer or tell it to the clerk, and the handbook adds that an answer on file is treated as an answer until a judge decides otherwise, even when it has no legal defense in it.

Typical defenses in the handbook include a landlord who lost the property to foreclosure and no longer owns it, a rent payment dropped off as the landlord instructed, and a termination that did not follow the lease. Public housing and subsidy tenants may have a right to an informal hearing first. A counterclaim might cover unmade repairs that damaged belongings. The answer must be truthful, since a knowingly false statement in a court filing can be a crime.

Is there any way back after a missed answer?

Rarely, and the handbook says so plainly. A tenant who was served by tack and mail and misses the deadline usually cannot count on more time, even after an emergency such as a hospital stay. A tenant who truly never learned of the papers can ask the court for permission to answer late or file a motion to set aside the judgment, explaining why no answer was filed and why the landlord should not be allowed to evict.

If a judge grants that order, the tenant should hand a copy to the landlord and keep one inside the rental in case the sheriff arrives. Payment of rent can also avoid a judgment, but only through the tender defense inside the seven day window. The handbook adds that even after a dismissal a landlord may file again later, so a won case does not end the dispute for good.

What changes when the rented house is sold or foreclosed?

A foreclosure ends the old landlord and tenant relationship, and the new owner can bring an eviction, though the new owner may instead create a fresh lease. The handbook warns that if a new owner demands or accepts rent while an eviction is under way, that can create a tenancy at will. Georgia Courts describes the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act as letting a tenant stay at least 90 days or through the rest of the lease, whichever is longer, with only 90 days if the buyer will live there.

Georgia Legal Aid adds the borrower's side. After a foreclosure sale the former owner no longer owns the home, and the buyer can file for eviction if the owner stays after a demand. The judge's ruling gives seven days to move, and the buyer may offer cash for keys, which usually means leaving the house empty and broom clean by an agreed date.

How does a sale of a tenant-occupied house work in Georgia?

The seller handles the tenant's deposit and, if a case is open, checks its status with the clerk before the closing. The handbook requires the old owner to pass the security deposit to the buyer or return it to the tenant, and a tenant can sue when neither happens. Ask a Georgia attorney whether the lease binds a buyer, since the handbook does not settle that.

The seller also owes the state transfer tax unless the contract says otherwise. The Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority says the tax is $1 for the first $1,000 and 10 cents for each additional $100 or fractional part, paid before the deed is recorded. Census figures put Georgia at 4,734,436 housing units in 2025, with 65.7 percent of homes owner occupied in 2020 to 2024.

Frequently asked questions

What is a dispossessory warrant in Georgia?

It is the court paper a landlord files to start an eviction. Georgia Courts says the affidavit, also called the warrant, asks the court to return the property to the landlord and award any unpaid rent. A landlord who does not get one cannot lawfully remove a tenant.

How soon after service must a tenant answer an eviction?

Within seven days of actual service, and the next business day when the seventh day is a Saturday, Sunday or holiday. The answer can be written or spoken to the clerk. A tenant who does not answer risks losing without a hearing.

Can a landlord collect rent when the tenant is served by tack and mail?

Not through a default. If the tenant never answers or appears after tack and mail service, the court can order the tenant out but cannot award rent or other money damages.

Who removes the tenant after the landlord wins?

Generally the sheriff supervises the removal after a writ of possession is issued, and the landlord pays the cost. The handbook says the tenant's belongings go on part of the landlord's land unless the landlord and officer agree on another spot. A tenant can still be removed after a judgment even if the tenant pays.

Does a foreclosure sale end a lease on a Georgia rental?

It ends the old landlord and tenant relationship, so the new owner can seek eviction or start a new arrangement. Georgia Courts says the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act can give a tenant at least 90 days or the rest of the lease. Ask the county magistrate court clerk or legal aid how it applies to a specific case.

What does a Georgia quitclaim deed actually transfer?

A Georgia quitclaim deed passes whatever interest the signer holds in the property and promises nothing about it. The Georgia Department of Revenue puts it plainly in its deed course material: if the grantor holds fee simple title, the grantee receives fee simple title, and if the grantor holds nothing, the grantee receives nothing.

That is the whole difference from a warranty deed. A warranty deed carries a covenant that the grantor really owns the land, which is why Georgia.gov calls warranty and limited warranty deeds usually the most reliable, though harder to negotiate. A quitclaim deed is easier to get from a seller, and the same page tells anyone accepting one to get protection such as title insurance first.

Because nothing is guaranteed, the deed is a tool for specific jobs rather than a general way to sell a house at full market confidence.

When do Georgia owners use a quitclaim deed?

Owners reach for a quitclaim deed when the title is murky or when no sale price is involved. The Department of Revenue course text lists the common uses.

  • Settling the affairs of a deceased owner when the quality of title is uncertain.
  • Resolving a boundary dispute where the property line is not clear.
  • Moving a spouse's interest to the other spouse, which transfers whatever interest the signer had.
  • Cancelling a security deed after a loan is paid, especially when the original security deed is lost.
  • Moving title after an involuntary sale, such as a sale on a judgment or a tax lien.

That last use is built into the tax sale statutes. When property is redeemed after a tax sale, O.C.G.A. 48-4-44 requires the tax sale purchaser to give the owner a quitclaim deed naming who paid the redemption money. Our Georgia tax sale guide covers how that redemption works.

What makes a quitclaim deed valid and recordable in Georgia?

A deed to land must be an original, written, and signed by the maker. O.C.G.A. 44-5-30 adds that it must be attested by an officer and by one other witness, and delivered to the buyer or the buyer's representative. The Department of Revenue course text summarizes this as two witnesses, one of whom is a notary public.

No special form is required. Under 44-5-33, a deed that makes the transaction clear is not defeated by a want of form, so a quitclaim deed can be short. The deed still needs consideration, with one exception: the same course text notes that a deed of gift does not require valuable consideration.

Recording adds a few mechanical rules under 44-2-14. The instrument must be an original that is attested or acknowledged as the law requires, and the name and mailing address of the natural person to receive it back must be printed or typed at the top of the first page. Skipping that return address does not by itself erase the filing, but clerks expect it.

A deed is recorded with the Clerk of Superior Court in the county where the land sits. Ask that clerk for current recording fees and any local formatting preferences.

How does transfer tax work on a quitclaim deed?

Georgia will not record a deed until the real estate transfer tax has been paid. The Department of Revenue says the clerk, or a deputy, then attaches a certification that the tax was paid. The Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority adds that this tax is an excise tax and not a property tax.

The Department of Revenue prints the rate as $1 for the first $1,000 or fractional part of $1,000, plus 10 cents for each additional $100 or fractional part of $100, based on the sale price. The person who executes the deed, or the person for whose benefit it is executed, owes the tax. The seller is liable, though contracts often shift the cost to the buyer.

Georgia law also requires the PT-61 declaration. The Authority runs a free online filing system with no account needed: you complete the form on its site, print a reference copy, and file it with the clerk along with the deed. No signatures are needed on the electronic form.

  • A PT-61 is required whenever ownership changes, even when no money moves, such as removing a name from a deed.
  • The Authority lists four categories that need no PT-61: security deeds, releases of security interest, leases other than a lease for years, and affidavits that do not transfer property.
  • Other exemptions from paying the tax still require the form to be filed.
  • A property that crosses county lines needs a deed and a PT-61 in each county, with the value pro-rated.
  • A transfer-on-death deed needs no PT-61 when recorded, but one is required after the owner dies and the beneficiary files an affidavit accepting the property.

For questions about what is taxable or exempt, the Department of Revenue says to ask the Clerk of Superior Court in your county.

What are the steps from signing to recording?

The sequence below follows the statutes and agency pages already cited. Each step is the owner's job unless a closing attorney handles it.

Georgia quitclaim deed steps and the official source for each
StepWhat happens
1. Prepare the deedOriginal, written, signed by the grantor; return address at top of page one
2. Witness itAttested by an officer plus one other witness
3. Complete the PT-61Filed online with the Clerks' Authority, then a reference copy is printed
4. Pay transfer taxPaid before recording; clerk certifies payment on the deed
5. Record the deedFiled with the Clerk of Superior Court in the county of the land

Does a seven year rule make a quitclaim deed enough to own the house?

No. Georgia.gov states that in the past a quitclaim deed gave full ownership after seven years of uncontested use, even when the person who gave you the deed was not the real owner, and that this is no longer so simple. More documentation than the deed alone is needed to be recognized as the owner.

The seven year period still appears in the law of prescription. The Department of Revenue course text explains that O.C.G.A. 44-5-164 allows title by prescription after seven years when the possessor holds a flawed written document, called color of title, and possession was public, continuous, exclusive, peaceable, and not merely permissive. Without color of title, 44-5-163 requires twenty years. Our Georgia adverse possession guide goes deeper on those periods.

For a seller, the practical point is that a quitclaim deed from a doubtful source does not cure a title problem on its own. A buyer or title insurer will look at the chain of title behind it.

How does a quitclaim deed fit into selling a Georgia house?

A quitclaim deed can move title between family members or clear a name before a sale, but a buyer receives no promise from it. Title insurance, which Georgia.gov recommends, is how buyers cover that gap, and insurers will examine the records behind the deed.

If you inherited a home with several heirs, or you are removing a former spouse from title, a quitclaim deed signed by that person may be the missing piece before you can list or sell. Each person with an interest usually has to sign for the buyer to receive the whole property. A Georgia real estate attorney can tell you whether a quitclaim deed, a warranty deed, or a court process fits your situation, and Georgia.gov points to the State Bar of Georgia for finding one.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a quitclaim deed in Georgia?

With the Clerk of Superior Court in the county where the land is located. Bring the original deed and the PT-61 reference copy, and have the transfer tax paid so the clerk can certify it.

Is a PT-61 form required if I am only adding or removing a name?

Yes. The Clerks' Authority says a PT-61 is required whenever ownership is changed, even without a payment, except for security deeds, releases of security interest, leases other than leases for years, and affidavits. Ask the clerk whether the tax itself is exempt.

Does a quitclaim deed protect the person who receives it?

No. It gives the grantee only what the grantor owns, with no warranty. Georgia.gov recommends title insurance and says a real estate attorney can help before you accept one.

Who pays the Georgia real estate transfer tax?

The seller is liable under the Department of Revenue's description, but a sales contract can assign the cost to the buyer. On a gift or family transfer, ask the Clerk of Superior Court whether an exemption applies.

Can I use a quitclaim deed to get my house back after a tax sale?

If you redeem the property after a tax sale, the purchaser must give you a quitclaim deed under O.C.G.A. 48-4-44. It should name the person who paid the redemption money, and it is recorded with the county clerk.

What is a transfer on death deed in Georgia?

A transfer on death deed, often shortened to TOD deed, lets a Georgia owner name who gets a piece of real estate after the owner dies, without a separate transfer during life. The rules sit in Chapter 17 of Title 44 of the Official Code of Georgia, Code Sections 44-17-1 through 44-17-7. The chapter first took effect on July 1, 2024 under SB 420, and HB 413 rewrote parts of it effective April 22, 2026.

The deed is recorded while the owner is alive, but it does nothing to the owner's rights until death. Under Code Section 44-17-7, the owner stays the legal and equitable owner and counts as an absolute owner with regard to creditors and purchasers. A house under a TOD deed can still be sold, mortgaged or leased by the owner without asking the person named in the deed.

Who can sign a Georgia TOD deed, and what does it need?

Only the record owner can sign it, and that owner needs the same legal capacity required to enter into a contract. An attorney in fact acting under a power of attorney is not authorized to sign one. Code Section 44-17-2 says the deed needs no consideration, so no payment has to change hands.

The deed is recorded with the clerk of superior court in the county where the land sits. A few points from the current text of Section 44-17-2:

  • The person named is called a grantee beneficiary, and the owner may name one or several.
  • The owner may name alternate beneficiaries who take only if a primary beneficiary dies first or dies before accepting the property.
  • A trustee of an express trust may be named as the beneficiary.
  • The deed cannot be used to create an express trust or a beneficial interest in real property under the trust code articles the statute cites.
  • No signature, consent or notice to the beneficiary is required while the owner is alive.
  • A real estate transfer tax declaration form is not filed with the deed itself.

How do you change or cancel a TOD deed?

You can revoke or replace it at any time before death, and the beneficiary does not have to agree. Section 44-17-4 sets two routes: record a revocation instrument, or record a later TOD deed. A later deed wipes out every earlier beneficiary designation for the same interest.

A revocation must refer to the original deed, carry the owner's signature, and have that signature attested by an officer as provided in Code Section 44-2-15 plus one other witness. Before the 2026 amendment the statute asked for two other witnesses, and an attorney in fact could also sign it. A will cannot revoke a recorded TOD deed, so a clause in a will naming someone else does not override it.

Selling the property during life ends the deed as well. Section 44-17-4(d) says that if the owner sells or conveys the interest, or moves it into the owner's own express trust, the TOD deed is revoked. It is also revoked if the only named beneficiary dies before accepting.

What happens to the house when the owner dies?

The beneficiary must take two steps after the death, and the title does not pass until both are complete. First, each beneficiary who wants the property signs an affidavit. Second, the affidavit is recorded. Under the 2026 text of Section 44-17-2, the property is not handed over automatically on the date of death.

The affidavit must verify the owner's death, say whether the owner and the beneficiary were married at the time of death, give the deed book and page of the recorded TOD deed, and include a legal description of the land. A copy of the death certificate is attached. For an owner who dies on or after July 1, 2026, the beneficiary records the affidavit, the real estate transfer tax declaration form and related papers with the clerk of superior court of the county where the land is located.

The earlier version of the statute gave beneficiaries nine months to record or the interest reverted to the estate. The current text of Section 44-17-2(e) no longer contains that deadline. Ask the clerk of superior court or a Georgia real estate attorney how a particular death date is handled, because the recording rule is tied to deaths on or after July 1, 2026.

What does the Georgia TOD deed process look like step by step?

Georgia TOD deed steps under O.C.G.A. Title 44, Chapter 17
StepWhat the code saysSection
Sign and record the deedRecord owner signs; recorded with the clerk of superior court; no consideration needed44-17-2(a)
Change courseRecord a revocation (officer plus one witness) or a later TOD deed44-17-4(a), (b)
Owner diesPersonal representative gives each beneficiary notice as under Code Section 53-5-844-17-2(g)(1)
Beneficiary acceptsExecute the affidavit, attach the death certificate, record it44-17-2(c) to (e)
Title passesProperty moves to the beneficiary subject to recorded liens and mortgages44-17-5(a)

Source: the 2025 Code of Georgia as amended by Ga. L. 2026, p. 15 (HB 413), reproduced at Justia.

Can a Georgia house under a TOD deed be sold?

Yes, at two different stages, and the paperwork differs. While the owner is alive, the owner sells as usual and signs the deed to the buyer, which revokes the TOD deed under Section 44-17-4(d).

After the death, the beneficiary can sell only once the acceptance affidavit is recorded, because that step moves the title out of the estate. A beneficiary who inherits a house with repairs, back taxes or a mortgage balance often wants a quick closing. We buy houses in Georgia as-is for cash, which can fit when the beneficiary lives out of town and does not want to manage a vacant property.

If the beneficiary has not accepted, the estate still holds the property. A personal representative of an insolvent estate that faces imminent foreclosure, condemnation or destruction may record an affidavit of notice with the lender's or government's notice attached. If no beneficiary has completed the acceptance steps, the representative can then sell the property, pay the debts, and return any remaining proceeds to the estate.

Who still has a claim on a house under a TOD deed?

The beneficiary takes the house subject to every recorded mortgage, lien, lease, easement and security deed that the owner made or was bound by. Section 44-17-5(a) lists recorded executory contracts of sale and options to purchase among them, and it covers any interest the owner conveyed that was smaller than the whole. A nonconsensual lien against the beneficiary does not attach until the acceptance affidavit is recorded.

Two points work in the beneficiary's favor. A person who became the owner's spouse after the TOD deed was signed cannot claim against it. The deed also takes priority over the unsecured debts of the owner's estate filed after death, unless the property is unredeemed.

  • Mortgage lenders keep their recorded security deeds.
  • Property tax liens stay ahead of the estate's repair lien described below.
  • A spouse who married the owner before the deed was signed is not cut off by the later-spouse rule.

What if a beneficiary dies first or the estate pays the bills?

If one of several beneficiaries dies before the owner, that share lapses and is split evenly among the surviving beneficiaries instead of going back to the estate. The same split applies to a beneficiary who dies after the owner but before accepting. If the deed names joint tenants with right of survivorship, a beneficiary's earlier death does not invalidate the joint tenancy for the others.

While the property waits for acceptance, a personal representative of a solvent estate may pay the mortgage, property taxes and repairs needed to keep the house from being destroyed. The estate is entitled to repayment and gets a priority special lien for any amount still unpaid one year after the beneficiary accepts. That lien is inferior to property tax liens and earlier recorded security deeds, and the estate has 30 days after the one-year mark to file a claim of lien with the clerk of superior court.

Frequently asked questions

Is a transfer on death deed legal in Georgia?

Yes. Georgia allows TOD deeds for real estate under O.C.G.A. 44-17-1 through 44-17-7, in effect since July 1, 2024 and amended by HB 413 effective April 22, 2026.

Does the beneficiary have to sign the TOD deed?

No. Section 44-17-2(b) says no signature, consent, agreement or notice to the beneficiary is required while the record owner is alive. The beneficiary signs only the acceptance affidavit after the owner's death.

Can a will override a TOD deed in Georgia?

No. Section 44-17-4(c) says a recorded TOD deed may not be revoked by the provisions of a will. The owner must record a revocation or a new TOD deed.

Where is the deed or affidavit recorded?

With the clerk of superior court in the county where the real estate is located. Ask that clerk's office for its recording requirements and fees.

Can I sell an inherited Georgia house before the affidavit is recorded?

Not as the beneficiary. Until acceptance is complete the property is still handled through the estate. Ask a Georgia probate or real estate attorney who can sign for the sale in your situation.

Which closing charges does Georgia law put on a seller?

One charge is set by the state itself: the real estate transfer tax. Attorney fees, the payoff of your mortgage and any agent commission come from your contract and your lender, so they differ from deal to deal.

Four items have official rules you can read before the day of closing. They are the transfer tax, the PT-61 form that travels with the deed, the property tax for the year, and withholding when the seller lives outside Georgia. The table further down lines them up side by side.

Request a draft settlement statement a few days ahead and check each line against the contract. Georgia lets buyer and seller agree to shift some of these costs, so the contract wording matters.

What is the formula for the Georgia transfer tax?

The state revenue agency bases the tax on the sale price: $1 covers the first $1,000 or any fraction of it, and each further $100 or fraction adds 10 cents. The authority is O.C.G.A. 48-6-1 through 48-6-10.

The tax is owed by the person who executes the deed or the one it benefits, and the agency names the seller as liable. The same page notes that contracts often shift the bill to the buyer. If your contract says nothing, the statute leaves it with you, which makes that clause worth reading before you sign.

The clerks' cooperative authority stresses that this is an excise tax on moving title and is separate from the yearly property tax. Paying it settles nothing about your county tax bill.

How does the PT-61 form fit into a Georgia closing?

The PT-61 declares the transfer for tax purposes, and a single form goes with each applicable deed. The filer completes it in the clerks' authority PT-61 eFiling portal, prints a copy, and takes that copy to the Clerk of Superior Court along with the deed documents.

Recording waits on payment of the transfer tax. Once it is paid, a certification of payment is attached by the clerk or a deputy. Whoever handles your closing normally prepares the form from settlement figures, so your job is to supply accurate sale and parcel details.

For help with the electronic process, the revenue agency lists customer support at (800) 304-5174, or (404) 327-9760 for local callers. For a taxability or exemption question, call the superior court clerk's office serving the house.

Where does the transfer tax money go after the clerk collects it?

The clerk splits it among three levels of government. The revenue agency's page says each Clerk of Superior Court must report the total transfer taxes distributed among the state, the county and the municipalities during the prior calendar year, on a form called FA-RETT, due March 1 each year.

That report is a clerk's duty and does not change what you owe at closing. What it shows is that the transfer tax is shared with the county and any city, and that the certification attached to your deed records that the tax was paid. Ask your settlement agent to confirm that the PT-61 is filed and the tax paid before the documents leave the table.

Who pays the property tax at a Georgia closing?

The person who held title on January 1 answers for that whole year's bill. The state notes that the rule holds even if the sale happens the next day, and that Georgia provides no refund of tax to partial-year owners.

The contract therefore decides how the year gets divided. Most counties set the due date at December 20, though some pick a different one, and taxpayers have 60 days after billing to pay. As one example of a different schedule, Fulton County made most 2026 bills due October 15, with the City of Atlanta's share due September 30.

Steps to take before closing:

  • Ask the tax commissioner of your county what the current bill stands at.
  • Ask your settlement agent how the contract splits the year.
  • Check that no county tax lien sits on the clerk's general execution docket, where such liens are filed.

Does the intangible recording tax land on the seller?

It attaches to a new long-term note secured by real estate, so it follows the buyer's financing. The rate is $1.50 per $500 of the note, or part of $500, up to a maximum of $25,000 on one note.

The lender has 90 days to record the security instrument, and the lender may pass the tax along to the borrower. Clerks of Superior Court collect it in most places. A list of 24 smaller counties, last updated July 2015, has the tax commissioner or tax collector doing it. The buyer's lender is the party that records the new security instrument.

When does Georgia withhold from a nonresident seller?

O.C.G.A. 48-7-128 makes the buyer withhold 3% of the price when the seller lives out of state, or 3% of the gain when the seller provides a sworn gain affidavit. Payment goes in by the end of the month after closing.

The state's exemptions include a principal residence under federal rules, prices below $20,000, and a transfer to a mortgagee in foreclosure with no added payment. Form IT-AFF3, the exemption certificate, is optional but helps the file. The agency's own FAQ describes the charge as income tax withholding.

Which closing records are worth keeping?

Hold on to the final settlement statement, the recorded deed information and any withholding statement the buyer gives you. A nonresident seller attaches the buyer's withholding return, or the equivalent document, to the Georgia income tax return to claim credit.

If a Form 1099-S arrives, the IRS says the sale is reportable even when the gain is excludable, and the settlement statement is what you check its figures against.

  • Final settlement statement showing price, payoff and every charge.
  • The PT-61 copy and the clerk's certificate that transfer tax was paid, when provided.
  • Property tax bill and payment proof for the year of sale.
  • Any Form G-2RP or similar statement of Georgia tax withheld.

Frequently asked questions

Who bears the transfer tax on a Georgia sale?

The seller, under the state's description, unless the contract moves it to the buyer, which is common. Read that clause before signing, since silence leaves the cost with the seller.

What is the Georgia transfer tax rate?

Georgia charges $1 on the first $1,000 and 10 cents on each additional $100, with fractions counted in full. The statutes run from O.C.G.A. 48-6-1 through 48-6-10, and your settlement statement shows the dollar figure.

Can a seller get back property tax after leaving mid-year?

No. Under the state's reading, ownership on January 1 fixes responsibility for the year, and a part-year owner is not refunded. Any split with the buyer happens through the contract.

Who files the PT-61 in Georgia?

The filer completes it online through the clerks' authority portal, and one form goes with each applicable deed. Ask your settlement agent to confirm who is preparing it and that it reaches the clerk with the deed.

Where do I ask about a transfer tax exemption?

Start with the superior court clerk in the property's county. The state sends taxability and exemption questions there, and the clerk certifies payment before the deed is recorded.

What is a tax lien on a Georgia house?

In Georgia a tax lien on real estate is called a fi. fa., short for fieri facias, and it is also called a tax execution. The Gwinnett County Tax Commissioner describes it as a claim on the property that lets the tax commissioner or the sheriff take whatever action the law allows to collect overdue taxes, and the first step toward a tax sale.

Some states package these liens and sell them to investors. Metro Atlanta counties work differently. Cobb County's tax commissioner states that the office does not sell tax liens and instead sells tax deeds at auction, and Gwinnett says it does not transfer liens in bulk to third-party investors. What a buyer gets at a Georgia sale is a tax deed, covered in our tax sale guide.

When does unpaid property tax turn into a lien?

The trigger is delinquency, and counties word it a little differently. DeKalb County says accounts with a balance after December 31 are subject to a lien, and that partial payments are accepted but penalties and interest keep accruing on what remains. Cobb County says unpaid taxes after the October 15 due date are subject to levy and tax sale.

Gwinnett adds a notice step for homes and land: for real property, the tax commissioner must send the owner a 30-day notice before filing the lien. Personal property liens can be filed any time after the account is delinquent.

Due dates differ by county and by year, so look at your own bill or ask the county tax commissioner before assuming a date.

What happens after the lien is filed?

A filed lien does not take the house by itself. The usual path runs through a levy, an advertisement, and an auction.

  • Lien filed. A filing fee is added to the account, and the lien stays until the taxes are paid in full.
  • Levy. Gwinnett explains that for real property a levy can be a posted sign. It does not change ownership and does not take away the owner's right to live there. Once levied, only certified funds are accepted and partial payments stop.
  • Selection for sale. Costs for title research and advertising are added. The owner can still pay everything owed to stop the sale.
  • Auction. The sale happens on the first Tuesday of a month, and the winning bidder receives a tax deed.

DeKalb notes that a lien may show up on credit reports even though the office does not report to credit agencies, and Gwinnett warns that a lien can complicate real property closings.

How do DeKalb, Cobb and Gwinnett handle delinquent accounts?

The same state statutes apply everywhere, but each tax commissioner publishes its own practices. The comparison below uses only what each county's own page states.

Delinquent tax practices published by three metro Atlanta tax commissioners
CountyLien timingSale location and payment
DeKalbBalances outstanding after December 31 are subject to a lienCourthouse steps, first Tuesday, April through December; cash, bank cashier's check or bank wire once scheduled
CobbUnpaid after the October 15 due date is subject to levy and saleSuperior Court Plaza on the first Tuesday of planned months; cash or certified check; tax deeds only
Gwinnett30-day notice for real property before a lien is filedIn front of the Justice and Administration Center in Lawrenceville; certified funds only

Other counties set their own routines, so call the tax commissioner for the parcel in question.

What charges get added on top of the unpaid tax?

The balance grows at each stage, which is why paying early is cheaper. DeKalb's conditions of sale list the opening bid as the original taxes, the late payment penalty, interest, the fi. fa. cost, an execution fee and other legal costs and fees the law allows.

  • Gwinnett adds a fi. fa. filing fee when the lien is filed.
  • Gwinnett adds levy costs and fees once a property is levied upon.
  • Once a property is picked for sale, Gwinnett adds costs for title research and advertising.
  • DeKalb keeps adding penalties and interest to any balance left after a partial payment.

Ask the tax commissioner for an itemized payoff before you list the house, so the figure in your sales contract matches what the county will actually require on the closing date.

Who is named on the lien if I sold the house during the year?

Georgia taxes accrue in full on January 1, so the January 1 owner carries the bill. Gwinnett's tax commissioner explains that both the seller and the new owner may receive a bill, and that a lien for unpaid taxes goes in the January 1 owner's name unless proof of the buyer's assumption is filed in time.

Three things must be in place within 90 days of the payment due date: acceptable proof that the purchaser assumed liability, a deed in the new owner's name, and proper recording of that deed. Wording matters. Gwinnett's examples of unacceptable contract language include general promises to prorate or to adjust between buyer and seller. Acceptable wording assigns the property tax liability to the purchaser, who agrees to pay it in full by the due date.

If the tax is paid on time, no paperwork is needed. If you are selling, ask the closing attorney to use clear assumption language and confirm the new deed is recorded.

How can I clear a lien before selling?

Payment of the outstanding taxes plus the fees, penalties and interest gets the lien marked satisfied, according to DeKalb. If a closing is coming, ask the tax commissioner for a payoff figure good through the closing date, and have the title company pay it from the proceeds.

Watch the payment form. After a property is scheduled for sale, DeKalb accepts only cash, bank-issued cashier's check or bank wire, and Gwinnett requires certified funds once the property is levied. Personal checks and cards will not do at that stage.

An older tax problem can also sit behind a current bill. DeKalb's delinquent report covers taxes due within the last seven years, and it warns that opening bids at a sale include all prior year taxes, so ask the office for anything older than that.

Is there a court-based alternative to a tax sale?

Yes. Georgia's judicial in rem foreclosure statutes, O.C.G.A. 48-4-75 through 48-4-81, let a county or city adopt a court process for delinquent property tax. A tax collector may not start one until 12 months after the taxes first became delinquent.

The proceeding enforces the lien only and does not create personal liability for the owner. Any interested party can redeem before the sale by paying the redemption amount. After a sale the owner has 60 days to redeem, and any amount bid above the minimum is placed with the superior court for distribution to interested parties, including the owner. Not every county has adopted this process, so ask the county tax commissioner which procedure applies.

Frequently asked questions

Can a Georgia tax lien stop me from selling my house?

It complicates the sale but does not block it. Gwinnett says liens can affect real property closing procedures, so the lien is normally paid off at closing and then marked satisfied.

Does a tax lien mean I lose my home right away?

No. A lien is the first step toward a sale. Gwinnett describes a real property levy as a posted sign that does not change ownership or the owner's right to live there, and a buyer at a sale still must wait out the redemption period.

Can I make partial payments on delinquent property tax?

DeKalb and Gwinnett both accept partial payments, but DeKalb says penalties and interest continue on the remainder, and Gwinnett says partial payments do not necessarily keep a property out of levy and sale. Once Gwinnett levies, partial payments stop.

Will a tax lien hurt my credit?

It can. DeKalb says its office does not report to credit agencies but that a lien may still appear on credit reports. Paying the balance in full gets the lien marked satisfied.

Do Georgia counties sell tax liens to investors?

Cobb states that it does not sell tax liens and instead sells tax deeds at auction, and Gwinnett says it does not transfer liens in bulk to investors. Ask your own county tax commissioner how it handles sales.

Which Georgia court handles probate?

The probate court in the county where the person lived at death. Georgia gives each county's probate court original jurisdiction over wills and the administration of estates, as the Georgia courts self-help page explains.

A layman's guide written by a retired probate judge and posted by Columbia County says the standard petitions use forms that are available at the courthouse and on the state probate courts' website. It adds that the forms suit simple filings, and anyone who finds the task harder than expected should consult an attorney. When a house is part of the estate, the same court rules on whether the personal representative may sell it.

How does a Georgia probate start when there is a will?

The person named as executor files a petition to probate the will, and the original signed will goes to the court with it. The guide names Standard Form 5 (Petition to Probate Will in Solemn Form) for that purpose, along with Standard Form 6, interrogatories to the will's witness.

Anyone holding a decedent's will must bring it to the probate court for filing, even when nobody plans to probate it. The petition lists the heirs by name, age, address and relationship, and the person signing swears to it before a notary or a probate clerk.

  • File in the county where the decedent was domiciled at death.
  • List every heir, including adopted children and children born outside marriage, but not stepchildren.
  • Expect the court to ask about any other will that someone may be offering elsewhere. The guide says that situation usually calls for an attorney.

What happens in Georgia when there is no will?

The probate judge appoints an administrator, who receives letters of administration showing authority over the estate. The petition is Standard Form 3, and the guide says anyone age 18 or older who is not incapacitated can serve, even if the person lives outside Georgia.

Heirs follow a set order. A surviving spouse and children come first, then parents, then siblings and their descendants, then grandparents, then aunts and uncles and their children, and finally the closest living relatives. A parent who willfully abandoned a minor child can lose that inheritance, though the guide says proving abandonment is work for an attorney.

An administrator normally posts a bond and files reports. If all heirs agree, the court can waive both, but notice of that request must be published in the county newspaper so creditors have a chance to object.

Can the estate's house be sold during Georgia probate?

Yes, but often only after the probate court gives permission. According to the guide, an intestate administrator, a temporary administrator and an executor all need leave to sell unless the will or the beneficiaries granted power to sell without advance approval.

The request for permission is Standard Form 13. The petition describes the property using the legal description from the recorded deed, states why the sale is needed, and says how the sale will happen and the lowest price acceptable. A contract already signed must be attached, and the guide says it should include a clause making the sale subject to court approval.

  • Attach a recent appraisal or the latest ad valorem tax statement for the property.
  • Raise the bond if needed so it covers the net sale proceeds.
  • Give notice to every heir or beneficiary. They may sign a notarized waiver, which the guide describes as far cheaper than sheriff service.
  • If an heir is a minor, incapacitated or cannot be found, the court appoints a guardian ad litem.

Rapid-sale petitions exist only for perishable personal property. Standard Form 15 does not cover a house.

Which Georgia probate petition fits which situation?

The court's standard forms are numbered, and the table below matches them to the situations a family selling inherited property usually faces.

Georgia probate standard forms mentioned in the Columbia County layman's guide

Form 3Petition for letters of administration (no will)
Form 5Petition to probate a will in solemn form
Form 10Petition for year's support
Form 13Personal representative's petition for leave to sell property
Form 15Leave to sell perishable personal property
Form 17Leave to convey or encumber property set aside as year's support

What is year's support in Georgia?

Year's support is an award of estate property to a surviving spouse, to minor children, or to both. It must be requested within 24 months of the date of death, in the probate court of the county where the decedent lived.

The guide lists two reasons families choose it. In many cases the decedent's creditors cannot reach property awarded this way, and a house awarded as year's support may not need back property taxes paid. It can be requested whether or not there is a will, but a spouse who remarried cannot receive it, and a child must be under 18 and unmarried.

Only property the decedent owned at death qualifies. A home held in joint tenancy with right of survivorship passes to the surviving joint owner and cannot be awarded. If no one objects after the hearing, the judge awards the property requested, and the certificate filed in superior court stands in place of a deed. A spouse or guardian who later wants to sell that property files Form 17.

Does Georgia charge an estate or inheritance tax?

No. The Department of Revenue states that Georgia has no inheritance tax and that, since July 1, 2014, the state levies no estate tax and requires no state estate tax return (O.C.G.A. 48-12-1).

The department adds that Georgia has no tax waiver requirement for transferring a decedent's stock or other assets. Anything owed to the IRS is a separate question, so ask the estate's accountant or the IRS whether a federal return applies.

Do transfer-on-death deeds and small-estate rules change the plan?

They can. The Department of Revenue's 2026 legislative update summarizes HB 413 on transfer-on-death deeds: a designated beneficiary has a right to a death certificate, the deed takes priority over unsecured debts, and revoking one now needs a single witness.

The same summary says no PT-61 transfer tax form is filed when the deed is recorded. The form is due only when the beneficiary later records an acceptance affidavit. The update also describes SB 403, which lets property of a deceased person held by the state as unclaimed property go out by affidavit instead of probate when it is under $7,500 and all heirs agree and sign. Ask the probate court clerk and the superior court clerk in the decedent's county how each step is handled locally.

Who pays property tax and transfer tax when an inherited Georgia house sells?

Whoever held title on January 1 is on the hook for that year's bill, and Revenue's FAQ says Georgia gives no refund for a partial year after a later sale. Before closing, ask the county tax commissioner for a payoff figure, and have the estate's representative confirm how the title company will handle it.

Real estate transfer tax is a separate charge, due before the superior court clerk records the deed. The state tax agency says the statute makes the seller liable, and buyers and sellers often shift it by contract. The estate's attorney or closing attorney can say which side pays on a given sale.

If the heirs are weighing a quick as-is sale, remember the sequence the guide lays out: appointment first, court permission where it applies, then notice to heirs, then closing.
