Frequently asked questions

Do I need a lawyer to open a Georgia probate case?

Not always. The probate courts publish standard forms meant for simple filings, but the layman's guide says to see an attorney when the filing gets harder than expected, when heirs cannot be found, or when someone disputes a will.

Can an heir sell the inherited house before probate is opened?

Ask the probate clerk in the decedent's county first. The layman's guide describes sales by a personal representative, after appointment and with court permission where required, so a buyer or title company will usually want that paperwork in place.

How long can a surviving spouse wait to request year's support?

Twenty-four months from the date of death. The petition is filed in the probate court of the county where the decedent lived, using Standard Form 10.

Does Georgia require the estate to pay a state tax before heirs receive property?

No. The Department of Revenue says Georgia has no estate or inheritance tax and does not require a tax waiver to transfer inherited assets.

Who must be notified when the personal representative asks to sell real estate?

Every heir if there is no will, or every beneficiary if there is a will. They can sign notarized waivers, and the court publishes notice in the county newspaper when an address is unknown.

Cash Home Buyers in Georgia

Georgia does not tax capital gains differently than other income, according to the Department of Revenue.

Is there a separate Georgia tax on profit from selling a house?

No separate tax exists. A Georgia taxpayer's gain lands on the regular state income tax return, because the Department of Revenue answers a direct question on the point with one line: the state does not tax capital gains differently than other income.

The Department's 2026 update page lists a flat income tax rate of 4.99%. It also lists standard deductions of $15,000 for single filers, heads of household and married people filing separately, and $30,000 for joint filers. Anything the page leaves open goes to the Taxpayer Services Division.

In practice the federal return does most of the sorting. If the IRS lets you exclude the profit on a main home, the amount that reaches Georgia is small or zero.

Will a federal exclusion shrink what Georgia sees?

Usually it does. The Georgia withholding guidance for nonresident sellers treats gain excluded from federal adjusted gross income as exempt, which tells you the state follows the federal treatment of a main residence.

The IRS exclusion tops out at $250,000 of gain for one filer or $500,000 on a joint return. Qualifying takes two things within the five years before closing: 24 months of ownership and 24 months of living in the house. Spouses on a joint return both need the living requirement, and a prior exclusion within the last two years can block a new one.

Publication 523 holds the worksheets. Military and some foreign service households can pause the five-year clock for as long as 10 years, according to the IRS.

How is any leftover gain measured and taxed federally?

The gain equals what you realized minus adjusted basis. Basis starts with your cost and rises with value-adding improvements, then falls with depreciation or insurance payments for casualty losses.

For tax years beginning in 2025, the IRS reports that most net capital gain is taxed at no more than 15% for most people, with a 0% bracket at the lower incomes shown below. A 20% rate applies above the 15% limits. Rented and depreciated houses can pull in a 25% maximum rate on the unrecaptured section 1250 portion. The IRS adds that losses on a personal home cannot be deducted.

Federal capital gains rate thresholds for tax years beginning in 2025, as printed in IRS Topic no. 409
Filing status0% rate up to15% rate up to
Single$48,350$533,400
Married filing jointly and qualifying surviving spouse$96,700$600,050
Head of household$64,750$566,700
Married filing separately$48,350$300,000

Which Georgia sellers have tax withheld at the closing table?

Nonresidents do. O.C.G.A. 48-7-128 makes the buyer hold back 3% of the price and send it to the state, and the seller later claims credit on a Georgia return.

The Department describes the exits:

  • A main home that qualifies under federal law is exempt for the gain federal law excludes.
  • A sworn gain affidavit, Form IT-AFF2, lets withholding drop to 3% of the gain.
  • Prices under $20,000 are exempt, and so are sales where the tax comes to less than $600 and the seller signs the affidavit.
  • A nonresident who meets every statutory condition can sign a deemed-resident affidavit.
  • Only net proceeds are withheld when 3% exceeds the cash due to the seller.

Remittance is due by the last day of the month after closing. A buyer who skips withholding can end up personally liable, so the closing office will ask for your residency facts early.

What papers should I gather before a gain is calculated?

Receipts shrink gains. Improvements add to basis, and the amount realized is figured after selling costs, so a tidy folder can lower the number you report.

  • The settlement statement from your purchase.
  • Invoices for work that added value, such as a new addition or a finished room.
  • Records of depreciation, casualty reimbursements or rental use.
  • Evidence of where you lived and when, such as utility bills, to prove the 24-month use test.
  • The final settlement statement from this sale, and a Form 1099-S if one arrives.

An heir or gift recipient follows separate basis rules, and the IRS sends such owners to Publication 551. Ask a tax preparer to confirm basis before pricing the house.

Do I owe estimated tax payments after a profitable sale?

Possibly. The IRS warns that anyone with a taxable capital gain may be required to make estimated tax payments, and it points to Publication 505 for the test. A big gain in a single quarter is the usual trigger, so ask a preparer about it before closing.

The IRS also notes that people with significant investment income may owe the net investment income tax, covered in its Topic no. 559. That is a federal layer on top of the rates in the table above.

On the Georgia side, the Department's update page gave April 15, 2026 as the no-extension deadline for 2025 individual returns, and it said most refunds go out within three weeks of receipt but can take up to 12 weeks. First-time filers, and people who have not filed in five or more years, get a paper refund check. A sale closed in a given calendar year is reported on the return filed the following spring, so set aside money from the proceeds for both returns before you spend the cash.

  • Ask whether your withholding or estimates already cover the gain.
  • Keep the withholding statement if the buyer held back 3% for Georgia.
  • Match the figures on your return to the final settlement statement.

When must I report a Georgia house sale to the IRS?

Report it whenever a Form 1099-S shows up, even if the entire profit is excludable. Report it as well when part of the profit exceeds the exclusion. Schedule D and Form 8949 are the IRS's named forms for the job.

The 1099-S is built from the settlement statement, so compare the sale price and the seller name on the statement with your own records. Ask the closing office to correct any mismatch before the form is filed.

Do older Georgia sellers or installment sales get special treatment?

Georgia gives taxpayers 62 or older, and those permanently and totally disabled, a retirement income adjustment. The Department includes capital gains income on the list of qualifying retirement income, next to pensions, interest, dividends and net rental income, and points to the Form IT-511 booklet for the yearly cap.

A sale paid out over several years is an installment sale. Under IRS rules you report gain as payments arrive unless you elect out by the return's due date, include interest as ordinary income, and keep the home exclusion available.

Frequently asked questions

What rate applies to capital gains in Georgia?

Georgia has no capital gains rate of its own. The Department of Revenue says gains are taxed like other income, and its 2026 update page lists a flat income tax rate of 4.99%.

How much profit on my Georgia house can I keep tax free?

Up to $250,000 as one filer or $500,000 on a joint return, when you meet the 24-month ownership and use tests. Publication 523 on irs.gov has the worksheets and the exceptions.

Does an out-of-state owner face withholding on a Georgia sale?

Often yes. The buyer withholds 3% of the price, or 3% of the gain with a sworn affidavit, unless an exemption applies. A qualifying main home is exempt for excluded gain, and prices under $20,000 are exempt.

Do I report the sale if no tax is due?

Yes when you get a Form 1099-S or when some gain cannot be excluded. The IRS names Schedule D and Form 8949 for that reporting.

What basis do I use for an inherited Georgia house?

Inherited property follows its own basis rules, which the IRS covers in Publication 551. Have a tax preparer confirm the figure before you set a price.

How does a Georgia tax sale work?

A Georgia tax sale is a public auction of a delinquent property after a tax lien has been issued and the property has been advertised. The winning bidder receives a tax deed, and the owner keeps a right to buy the property back. Sales run under O.C.G.A. 48-3-1 and 48-4-1 and following, as the DeKalb County conditions of sale state.

The county sets the calendar. DeKalb holds sales on the first Tuesday of the month from April through December on the courthouse steps in Decatur. Cobb holds them on the first Tuesday of the months it plans a sale, moving to Wednesday if Tuesday is a holiday. Gwinnett says it generally holds sales in only a few selected months.

Opening bids are the unpaid taxes plus penalties, interest, and costs. Georgia sells the deed, and the lien itself is not what changes hands, a point Cobb stresses by stating that it sells tax deeds and does not sell tax liens.

What does a bidder have to do on sale day?

Registration comes first. Cobb requires pre-registration for each sale and issues bidder cards between 9:00 and 10:00 a.m. on the day, against a photo ID. DeKalb requires registration for each sale as well, either online beforehand or in person that morning.

  • Payment. Cobb wants payment in full when the sale ends, by cash or certified check. DeKalb's conditions require cash, a cashier's check or a certified check from an insured institution within one hour after the sale ends.
  • Failure to pay. DeKalb says an unpaid bid goes back up for resale the same afternoon, and the defaulting bidder may owe the difference or be barred from later sales.
  • Unsold parcels. Cobb may re-auction properties that drew no bid at 3 p.m. that afternoon.
  • Buyer beware. DeKalb's conditions state that the doctrine of caveat emptor applies to every tax sale.

For an owner, the same details matter in reverse: once a sale is scheduled, DeKalb accepts only cash, bank cashier's checks or bank wires, and Gwinnett accepts only certified funds.

How long can the owner take the property back?

At least 12 months, and often longer. O.C.G.A. 48-4-40 lets the defendant in the execution, or anyone with a right, title, interest or lien in the property, redeem within 12 months of the sale, and after that until the right is cut off by the statutory notice.

Georgia's redemption price is set by 48-4-42. The table below lists the pieces as the Department of Revenue course text prints them for sales after July 1, 2002.

What the redemption payment includes under O.C.G.A. 48-4-42
ComponentRule as printed
BidThe amount paid at the tax sale, as shown in the tax deed
Later taxesAny taxes the purchaser paid after the sale
Special assessmentsAny special assessments on the property
Premium20 percent for the first year or fraction of a year since the sale, then 10 percent for each additional year or fraction of a year
Notice costsSheriff's cost for serving the notice and publication costs, if redemption comes more than 30 days after the foreclosure notice
Association sumsFor sales after July 1, 2016, certain amounts paid to a property owners', condominium or homeowners' association

Payment goes to the purchaser in lawful United States money. Cobb adds that the tax sale purchaser is responsible for working out the redemption amount, so ask the purchaser or the tax commissioner for a written figure.

Can the purchaser move in right after the sale?

No. Cobb's tax commissioner states that the purchaser gets a tax deed but cannot take possession, make improvements, evict tenants or move onto the property. Gwinnett says buyers at a sale do not automatically own the property and owners are not immediately evicted.

The purchaser can end the owner's right to redeem only by following the notice rules in 48-4-45. After 12 months the purchaser serves notice on the defendant in the execution, the occupant, and everyone with a recorded interest or lien in the county, and must publish it once a week for four consecutive weeks in the sheriff's advertisement newspaper. Notice to people outside the county goes by registered or certified mail or statutory overnight delivery.

Even then the deed is not final overnight. Under 48-4-48 a tax deed executed at a valid sale after July 1, 1996 ripens into fee simple title four years after the deed is recorded in the county land records.

What if I redeem the property or the sale brings in extra money?

Redemption puts the title back in the owner, subject to every lien that existed at the time of the sale, according to 48-4-43. The purchaser must then sign a quitclaim deed to the owner under 48-4-44, naming who paid the redemption money. If it is not presented at redemption, the purchaser has seven days to supply one properly witnessed, and it must reach the clerk of the superior court within ten days of the redemption. Our quitclaim deed guide explains that kind of deed.

When a sale brings in more than taxes and costs, the extra money belongs to the parties with an interest. Cobb says its tax commissioner may file an interpleader in superior court to distribute it, and DeKalb holds excess funds until a rightful party files a claim. DeKalb accepts claims only from the entitled party or a Georgia attorney, and not from an agent under a power of attorney.

How does the court-supervised sale differ?

Counties and cities that adopt the process under 48-4-76 can foreclose through superior court instead. The sale is advertised as sheriffs' sales are, cannot occur earlier than 45 days after the court's order, and the minimum bid is the redemption amount.

The owner's redemption window is shorter, 60 days after the sale, and the owner redeems by paying the minimum bid price into the superior court. Within 90 days after the sale, the petitioner must deliver the deed and file a report of the sale. Any surplus above the minimum bid is deposited with the court and distributed by priority to the interested parties, including the owner.

Can I sell my Georgia house before a tax sale?

Yes, a sale to a buyer that closes before the auction can pay the delinquent taxes out of the proceeds. The county will treat payment of everything owed as a stop to the sale, and Gwinnett confirms that the owner can pay all taxes, costs and fees after a property is selected for sale, in certified funds. Ask the tax commissioner for a payoff figure through your closing date, since advertising and title research fees keep being added as the sale approaches.

If the auction has already taken place, the 12 month redemption period is the next deadline. A buyer purchasing from you then has to account for the purchaser's rights as well, so involve a Georgia real estate attorney and a title company early.

Frequently asked questions

Where are Georgia tax sales held?

At the county, usually at the courthouse. DeKalb holds them on the courthouse steps in Decatur, Cobb at the Superior Court Plaza, and Gwinnett in front of the Justice and Administration Center in Lawrenceville.

How long do I have to redeem after a Georgia tax sale?

At least 12 months from the sale date. After that the right continues until the purchaser cuts it off by giving the statutory foreclosure notice to the owner, the occupant and recorded interest holders.

What does redemption cost?

The purchaser's bid, plus later taxes the purchaser paid, special assessments, and a premium of 20 percent for the first year or fraction and 10 percent for each additional year or fraction. Notice costs may be added. Get the exact figure in writing.

Does the buyer at a tax sale own the house immediately?

No. The buyer holds a tax deed that works like a lien until redemption rights end. Cobb says the purchaser cannot take possession, improve the property or evict tenants during that time.

What happens to extra money from a tax sale?

It is held for the parties entitled to it. DeKalb takes claims from the entitled party or a Georgia attorney, and Cobb may file an interpleader action in superior court to distribute the money.
